A type of anemia characterized by increased size of erythrocytes with increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and increased mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH).
The presence of abnormally shaped erythrocytes.
Hemorrhage affecting the gingiva.
Recurrent or excessive bleeding from the mouth.
Abnormally increased variability in the size of erythrocytes.
Abnormal loss of protein from the digestive tract related to excessive leakage of plasma proteins into the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract.
A bacterial infection and inflammation of the skin und subcutaneous tissues.
Warts, benign growths on the skin or mucous membranes that cause cosmetic problems as well as pain and discomfort. Warts most often occur on the hands, feet, and genital areas.
A lasting absence of total IgG and total IgA and total IgM in the blood circulation, whereby at most trace quantities can be measured.
An abnormality of T cells.

Pulmonary bullae are rounded focal regions of emphysema with a thin wall which measure more than 1 cm in diameter. They are often subpleural in location and are typically larger in the apices. In some cases, bullae can be very large and result in compression of adjacent lung tissue. A giant bulla is arbitrarily defined as one that occupies at least one third of the volume of a hemithorax. When large, bullae can simulate pneumothorax. The most common cause is paraseptal emphysema but bullae may also be seen in association with centrilobular emphysema.
An increased susceptibility to lower respiratory tract infections as manifested by a history of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections.
The presence of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins) in the serum that react to thyroglobulin.
Abnormal reduction in the count of eosinophils in the blood per volume.
An increase in the thickness of the pleura, generally related to scarring of the pleural tissue.
An abnormally decreased concentration of interleukin 10 in the blood circulation.
An abnormally decreased concentration of interleukin 21 in the blood circulation.
An abnormally decreased concentration of interleukin 22 in the blood circulation.
An abnormally decreased concentration of interleukin 27 in the blood circulation.
An abnormally decreased concentration of interleukin 17A in the blood circulation.
An abnormally decreased concentration of interleukin 23 in the blood circulation.
An abnormally increased level of immunoglobulin G in blood.
An abnormally increased overall level of immunoglobulin E in blood.
An abnormally increased level of immunoglobulin A in blood.

A chronic granulomatous inflammatory disease of the intestines that may affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus, causing a wide variety of symptoms. It primarily causes abdominal pain, diarrhea which may be bloody, vomiting, or weight loss, but may also cause complications outside of the gastrointestinal tract such as skin rashes, arthritis, inflammation of the eye, tiredness, and lack of concentration. Crohn's disease is thought to be an autoimmune disease, in which the body's immune system attacks the gastrointestinal tract, causing inflammation.
A type of neutropenia that is observed in the presence of granulocyte-specific antibodies.

A reduction in the normal proportion of class-switched memory B cells (CD19+/CD27+/IgM+/IgD+) relative to the total number of B cells. Marginal zone B cells undergo limited somatic hypermutation and produce high-affinity IgM and some IgG, whereas class-switched memory B cells synthetize IgG, IgM, and IgA.
Atrophy of the kidney.

Abnormality of the growth of secondary sexual hair, which normally ensues during puberty. In males, secondary sexual hair usually comprises body hair, including underarm, abdominal, chest, and pubic hair. In females, secondary sexual hair usually comprises a lesser degree of body hair, most prominently underarm and pubic hair.
Absence or developmental hypoplasia of the uterus.
Aplasia, that is failure to develop, of the ovary.
An elevated concentration of follicle-stimulating hormone in the blood.
Reduced number or density of pubic hair.
An elevated concentration of luteinizing hormone in the blood.
Osteoporosis affecting predominantly the vertebrae.
Absence or underdevelopment of the breasts.
Abnormal largeness of the eye with an axial length > 2.5 standard deviations from population mean.
A severe form of sensorineural hearing impairment.
An abnormal increase in the size of the foramen magnum.
Developmental hypoplasia of the antihelix.
An abnormally low volume of the white matter of the brain.
The ability of the wrist joints to move beyond their normal range of motion.

A type of focal motor seizure characterized by sudden, brief (<100 ms) involuntary single or multiple contraction(s) of muscles(s) or muscle groups of variable topography (axial, proximal limb, distal). Myoclonus is less regularly repetitive and less sustained than is clonus.
Eyelashes that draw the attention of the viewer due to increased density and/or length and/or curl without meeting the criteria of trichomegaly.
Protrusion of the meninges through a defect of the skull or vertebral column.
A form of lissencephaly characterized by an uneven cortical surface with a so called 'cobblestone' appearace. There are no distinguishable cortical layers.
A structural abnormality of the pons.
An abnormal predominance of type I muscle fibers (in general, this feature can only be observed on muscle biopsy).
Muscle hypertrophy affecting the calf muscles.
Reduced strength of the axial musculature (i.e., of the muscles of the head and neck, spine, and ribs).
Weakness of the limb-girdle muscles (also known as the pelvic and shoulder girdles), that is, lack of strength of the muscles around the shoulders and the pelvis.

A facial appearance characteristic of myopathic conditions. The face appears expressionless with sunken cheeks, bilateral ptosis, and inability to elevate the corners of the mouth, due to muscle weakness.
Increased susceptibility to fatigue.

A compound muscle action potential (CMAP) is a type of electromyography (EMG). CMAP refers to a group of almost simultaneous action potentials from several muscle fibers in the same area evoked by stimulation of the supplying motor nerve and are recorded as one multipeaked summated action potential. This abnormality refers to a greater than normal decrease in the amplitude during the course of the investigation.

An abnormality of the ability (skills) to perform a precise movement of large muscles with the intent to perform a specific act. Gross motor skills are required to mediate movements of the arms, legs, and other large body parts.

A progressive disorder of vertebral joint degeneration that occurs in the setting of any condition characterized by decreased afferent innervation, involving loss of deep pain and proprioceptive sensation in the vertebral column. Patients most commonly present with symptoms of lower back pain, sitting imbalance, progressive spinal deformity (usually kyphosis), and an audible clicking sound on changing postures.
Generalized (unlocalized) atrophy affecting muscles of the limbs in both proximal and distal locations.
Reduced ability to run.
Generalized weakness of the muscles of the arms and legs.
Hypoplasia of the cerebellum, pontine nuclei, and inferior olivary nucleus.

Unusual regions of densely packed membranous tubules known as tubular aggregates which present as membranous inclusions, derived from membranes of sarcoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, containing miscellaneous proteins with a variety of enzymatic activities.

Immunohistochemistry reveals reduced alpha dystroglycan protein in the muscle biopsy. Alpha-dystroglycan is a heavily glycosylated peripheral-membrane component of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex (DAPC), which, in addition to laminin alpha2, binds perlecan and agrin in the extracellular matrix, whereas beta-dystroglycan, derived from the same gene, is a transmembrane protein that links to dystrophin intracellularly.
A reduction in the degree of glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan in muscle tissue.

The variation in the time interval between the two action potentials of the same motor unit is called jitter. This term therefore applies to increased variability in the interval between successive action potentials of the same motor unit, which is measured by electromyography (EMG).
Improvement of muscle strength in response to administration of an acetylcholine esterase inhibitor.
A type of weakness of skeletal muscle that occurs after a muscle group is used and lessens if the muscle group has some rest. That is, there is diminution of strength with repetitive muscle actions.
An anomaly in the communication from a neuron to a target across a synapse in the peripheral nervous system.
Increased time between the start of the Q wave and the end of the T wave as measured by the electrocardiogram (EKG).
A localized outpouching of ventricular cavity that is generally associated with dyskinesia and paradoxical expansion during systole.
An abnormal closure, or atresia of the tubular structure of the ileum.
Abnormal outpouching or sac-like dilatation in the wall of an atery, vein or the heart.

Recurrent attacks of acute inflammatory arthritis of a joint or set of joints caused by elevated levels of uric acid in the blood which crystallize and are deposited in joints, tendons, and surrounding tissues.
Vomiting that ejects the gastric contents with great force.
Elevations of the levels of SGOT (serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase) and SGPT (serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase) that occur during infections.
An abnormality of coagulation related to a decreased concentration of vitamin K-dependent protein S. Protein S is a cofactor of protein C.

Abnormal transferrin isoform profile consistent with a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. In the traditional nomenclature for congenital disorders of glycosylation, absence of entire glycans was designated type I, and loss of one or more monosaccharides as type II.

An abnormality of coagulation related to a decreased concentration of vitamin K-dependent protein C. Protein C is activated to protein Ca by thrombin bound to thrombomodulin. Activated protein C degrades factors VIIIa and Va.
An abnormality of coagulation related to a decreased concentration of antithrombin-III.
Decreased activity of coagulation factor XI. Factor XI, also known as plasma thromboplastin antecedent, is a serine proteinase that activates factor IX.
Reduced antithrombin antigen. A reduced level of antithrombin may lead to an increased risk of thrombus formation.

An elevation of the blood concentration of an androgen, that is, of a steroid hormone that controls development and maintenance of masculine characteristics. The androgens include testosterone and Dehydroepiandrosterone.
Well-demarcated area(s) of partial or complete depigmentation in the fundus, reflecting atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium with associated retinal photoreceptor loss.
Abnormality of left ventricular contraction, often defined operationally as an ejection fraction of less than 40 percent.
Increased size of cerebral gyri, often associated with a moderate reduction in the number of sulci of the cerebrum.
Underdevelopment of part or all of the male external reproductive organs (which include the penis, the scrotum and the urethra).
Absence or underdevelopment of the musculature.
A condition in which the anterior part of the foot rotates outward away from the midline of the body and the heel remains straight.
Muscular atrophy in the distribution of shoulder girdle and peroneal muscles.
An anomaly of the vermis of cerebellum.

A congenital abnormality of the cerebral hemisphere characterized by lack of gyrations (convolutions) of the cerebral cortex. Agyria is defined as cortical regions lacking gyration with sulci great than 3 cm apart and cerebral cortex thicker than 5 mm.
A form of anterior segment dysgenesis in which abnormal cleavage of the anterior chamber occurs. Peters anomaly is characterized by central, paracentral, or complete corneal opacity.
A kinked appearance of the brainstem, i.e., an exaggerated flexure.
A deviation from the normal serum concentration/activity of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), which catalyzes the reduction of pyruvate to form lactate.
Abnormal development of the choroid and retina.
The presence of developmental dysplasia of the retina.

An abnormal concentration of aldolase in the serum. Aldolase is an enzyme responsible for converting fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into the triose phosphates dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.
Abnormality of the optic nerve.
Diffusely large eye (with megalocornea) associated with glaucoma.
A decreased concentration of citrulline in the blood.
Abnormal acid accumulation or depletion of base.

Epilepsia partialis continua (also called Kojevnikov's or Kozhevnikov's epilepsia) is a type of focal motor status epilepticus characterized by repeated stereotyped simple motor manifestations such as jerks, typically of a limb or the face, recurring every few seconds or minutes for extended periods (days or years).

Hemiballismus is a rare movement disorder that is caused primarily by damage to various areas in the basal ganglia. Hemiballismus is usually characterized by involuntary flinging motions of the extremities. The movements are often violent and have wide amplitudes of motion. They are continuous and random and can involve proximal and/or distal muscles on one side of the body, while some cases even include the facial muscles. The more a patient is active, the more the movements increase. With relaxation comes a decrease in movements.
Abnormally decreased levels of serine in cerebrospinal fluid.
The condition of inability to eat normally treated by placement of a thin tube through the nose into the stomach that is then used to carry food.
Abnormally decreased levels of glycine in cerebrospinal fluid.
Sudden-onset episode of abnormal, involuntary eye movements.
Increased susceptibility to upper and lower respiratory tract infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of upper and lower respiratory tract infections.
This term refers to a phenotypic feature that was first observed prior to birth during the third trimester, which is defined as 28 weeks and zero days (28+0) of gestation and beyond.
Death during adolescence, the period between childhood and adulthood (roughly between the ages of 10 and 19 years).
The presence of chyle (a type of lipid-rich lymph) in the pleural space (the space surrounding the lung) as observed in a fetus.

Fetal pleural effusion is the accumulation of excess fluid in the layers of tissue (pleura) lining the lungs and wall of the chest. It may be primary, also termed hydrothorax, occurring as an isolated finding or it may be secondary, most commonly resulting from non-immune hydrops.
Accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity during the fetal period.
Partial or complete wasting (loss) of hippocampus tissue that was once present.
The pinna has fewer folds and grooves than usual.
Forward protrusion of the glabella.
An overlap of the bony plates of the skull in an infant, with or without early closure.
A condition in which the superior portion of the helix is folded over to a greater degree than normal.
Inability of velopharyngeal sphincter to sufficiently separate the nasal cavity from the oral cavity during speech.
The presence of an abnormally prominent antihelix.

Reduced muscle tone of oral musculature. In infants, this feature may be associated with difficulties in breast feeding, and may affect the latch, jaw motions, tongue placement, lip seal, suck/swallow/breathe pattern and overall feeding behavior.
The presence of a diverticulum (sac or pouch) in the wall of the urethra.
An abnormally increased ability of the skin to permit light to pass through (translucency) such that subcutaneous structures such as veins display an increased degree of visibility.
Prominent positioning of the premaxilla in relation to the rest of the maxilla, the facial skeleton, or mandible. Not necessarily caused by an increase in size (hypertrophy of) the premaxilla.
Loss of elasticity of the upper and lower eyelids causing the skin to sag and bulge.
A scar refers to a lesion in which wound, burn, or sore has not healed completely and fibrous connective tissue has developed.
Abnormal tortuous (i.e., twisted) form of arteries affecting most or all arteries.
An aneurysm (severe localized balloon-like outward bulging) in the pulmonary artery.
Abnormal twisting of arteries or veins.
An abnormal widening of the diameter of the pulmonary artery.
Presence of a many diverticula (sac or pouch) in the wall of the urinary bladder.

An abnormality of the skull, the bony framework of the head which is comprised of the neurocranium (with eight cranial bones) and the viscerocranium (facial skeleton) that comprises fourteen facial bones with the mandible as its largest bone.
An abnormality of the cardiac ventricular function.
Subjective impression of increased softness upon palpation of the skin.
An abnormality of the face.
Abnormal tortuous (i.e., twisted) form of arteries.
A type of asthma in which aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) that inhibit cyclooxygen-ase 1 (COX-1) exacerbate bronchoconstriction.

Distant, or disseminated infection with Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) following vaccination associated with failure to contain thebacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) following vaccination leading to spread of BCG to many sites in the body. The tuberculosis vaccine BCG contains live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis.
Tightening of smooth muscle surrounding the bronchi and bronchioles with consequent wheezing and shortness of breath.
Increased count of eosinophils in the blood.

Degeneration (wear and tear) of articular cartilage, i.e., of the joint surface. Joint degeneration may be accompanied by osteophytes (bone overgrowth), narrowing of the joint space, regions of sclerosis at the joint surface, or joint deformity.
Increased concentration of ferritin in the blood circulation.
An above normal level of saturation of serum transferrin with iron.

An exaggerated whealing tendency when the skin is stroked, that is, formation of red, itchy bumps and lines on the skin as a result of pressure on the skin (for instance, stroking the skin with a pen or tongue depressor).
Redness of the skin of the face, caused by hyperemia of the capillaries in the lower layers of the skin.
Raised, well-circumscribed areas of erythema and edema involving the dermis and epidermis. Urticaria is intensely pruritic, and blanches completely with pressure.
Bipolar disorder is an illness of mood characterized by alternating episodes of elevated and depressed moods, which are interspersed with euthymic periods.

Partial or complete wasting (loss) of muscularois propria tissue that was once present. The atrophy may involve a marked vacuolar degeneration of myocytes, loss of muscle fibers and some cases a highly characteristic honeycomb fibrosis.
An abnormal, increased fatiguability of the musculature.
A type of dysmetria involving the limbs.
A type of myopathy associated with mitochondrial disease and characterized by findings on biopsy such as ragged red muscle fibers.

Impaired ability to repeat non-word sounds. The test for nonword repetition involves the repetition of nonsensical words of increasing length and complexity and is regarded as a measure of phonological (speech sound) processing and short-term memory
Inability to elicit tendon reflexes in the lower limbs.
Abnormally increased production of urine during the night leading to an unusually frequent need to urinate.
Any anomaly of cell structure.

An anomaly of the mitochondrion, the membranous cytoplasmic organelle the interior of which is subdivided by cristae. The mitochondrion is a self replicating organelle that is the site of tissue respiration.
Dysfunction of the proximal tubule, which is the portion of the duct system of the nephron of the kidney which leads from Bowman's capsule to the loop of Henle.
A form of hepatic steatosis characterized by the presence of large, lipid-laden vesicles in the affected hepatocytes.

Rickets is divided into two major categories including calcipenic and phosphopenic. Hypophosphatemia is described as a common manifestation of both categories. Hypophosphatemic rickets is the most common type of rickets that is characterized by low levels of serum phosphate, resistance to ultraviolet radiation or vitamin D intake. There are several issues involved in hypophosphatemic rickets such as calcium, vitamin D, phosphorus deficiencies. Moreover, other disorder can be associated with its occurrence such as absorption defects due to pancreatic, intestinal, gastric, and renal disorders and hepatobiliary disease. Symptoms are usually seen in childhood and can be varied in severity. Severe forms may be linked to bowing of the legs, poor bone growth, and short stature as well as joint and bone pain. Hypophosphatemic rickets are associated with renal excretion of phosphate, hypophosphatemia, and mineral defects in bones. The familial type of the disease is the most common type of rickets.
A progressive form of decreased height of the intervertebral disk.
A reduced number of large myelinated nerve fibers.
The presence of multiple deletions of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA).
A severe form of lactic acidemia.
A diminution of the volumetric fraction of blood pumped out of the ventricle with each cardiac cycle.
An inability of the tubules in the kidney to reabsorb small molecules, causing increased urinary loss of electrolytes (sodium, potassium, bicarbonate), minerals, glucose, amino acids, and water.

An abnormality of the spinocerebellar tracts, a set of axonal fibers originating in the spinal cord and terminating in the ipsilateral cerebellum. The spinocerebellar tract convey information to the cerebellum about limb and joint position (proprioception). They comprise the ventral spinocerebellar tract, the anterior spinocerebellar tract, and the posterior spinocerebellar tract.

Abnormal small intestinal contractions, such as spasms and intestinal paralysis related to the loss of the ability of the gut to coordinate muscular activity because of endogenous or exogenous causes.
An abnormality of an extraocular muscle.
An impairment of the electrical continuity between the atria and ventricles.

Third-degree atrioventricular (AV) block (also referred to as complete heart block) is the complete dissociation of the atria and the ventricles. Third-degree AV block exists when more P waves than QRS complexes exist and no relationship (no conduction) exists between them.
Initial bilateral ptosis followed by limitation of eye movements in all directions and slowing of saccades.
Paralysis of the external ocular muscles.
An abnormally reduced proportion of naive CD8 T cells relative to the total number of T cells.
Any abnormality in the proportion of naive CD4 T cells relative to the total number of T cells.
Abnormally wide morphology of the proximal epiphysis of the femur.
A disorder of bone growth affecting the vertebrae and the ends of the long bones (epiphyses).
Sclerosis (hardening) of the arteries with increased thickness of the wall of arteries as well as increased stiffness and a loss of elasticity.
An abnormality of morphology of primary molar.
An abnormality of the femoral head.
An abnormal deviation from normal levels of immunoglobulins in blood.
A type of disproportionate short stature characterized by a short trunk but a average-sized limbs.
Arteriosclerosis (increased thickness, increased stiffness, loss of elasticity) of the small arteries of the brain.
Underdevelopment of the proximal epiphysis of the femur.
A developmental anomaly with lateral displacement of the femoral head.
Reduced transparency of the stroma of cornea.
An abnormal functionality of the thyroid gland.
Microscopic hematuria detected by dipstick or microscopic examination of the urine.
A primary immune deficiency that is characterized by defects or deficiencies of T-lymphocytes that causes specific susceptibility to intracellular micro-organisms.
Severely increased amount of excretion of protein in the urine, defined as 3.5 grams per day or more in adults and 40 mg per meter-squared body surface area per hour in children.
A type of lymphoma characterized microscopically by the absence of multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells.
Developmental delay of ossification of the proximal epiphysis of the femur.
A pregnancy that extends to 42 weeks of gestation or beyond.
An abnormal elevation of the concentration of thyroglobulin, a protein produced in the thyroid gland that acts as a precursor to thyrroid hormones.
A deviation from the normal concentration of thyroglobulin, a protein produced in the thyroid gland that acts as a precursor to thyrroid hormones.

An abnormal result of the perchlorate discharge test. In this test, first radioactive iodine is administered, sufficient time is allowed to pass so that the radioactive iodine is captured by the thyroid,and then, perchlorate is administered orally. The perchlorate displaces non-organified iodide from the thyroid. The perchlorate discharge test is considered positive (abnormal) if there is an abnormally rapid loss of radioactive iodine from the thyroid.

A decreased amount of uptake on the radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) test, which utilizes a radioisotope of iodine to measure how much iodine the thyroid gland absorbs from the blood. The radioactive marker is measured 4-6 hours and in some cases also 24 hours after administration of the radioactive marker.

An elevated amount of uptake on the radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) test, which utilizes a radioisotope of iodine to measure how much iodine the thyroid gland absorbs from the blood. The radioactive marker is measured 4-6 hours and in some cases also 24 hours after administration of the radioactive marker.

Any deviation from normal in the amount of uptake on the radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) test, which utilizes a radioisotope of iodine to measure how much iodine the thyroid gland absorbs from the blood. The radioactive marker is measured 4-6 hours and in some cases also 24 hours after administration of the radioactive marker.

An anomaly of epiphysis, which is the expanded articular end of a long bone that developes from a secondary ossification center, and which during the period of growth is either entirely cartilaginous or is separated from the shaft by a cartilaginous disk.
Excessive sleepiness or feeling of sleepiness, or difficulty staying awake despite having had adequate sleep, which persists over several days.
Patchy and irregular skin pigmentation.
A type of hyperbilirubinemia with neonatal onset.

A reduction below the normal concentration of thyroxine in the blood. Thyroxine (also known as T4) is the main hormone secreted by the thyroid gland into the blood. It can be converted into the active form triiodothyronine (also known as T3).
Underdevelopment (hypoplasia) of the big toe.
Medial deviation of the great toe owing to a deformity of the great toe joint causing the hallux to deviate medially.
Chronic hepatitis associated with infection by cryptosporidia, as demonstrated (for example) by immunohistochemistry of liver tissue.

An opportunistic disease caused by invasion of unicellular fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii. Transmission of P. jirovecii cysts takes place through the airborne route, and usually, its presence in lungs is asymptomatic. However, people with impaired immunity, especially those with CD4+ T cell count below 200/microliter, are still at risk of the development of Pneumocystis pneumonia due to P. jirovecii invasion. Symptoms induced by this disease are not specific: progressive dyspnoea, non-productive cough, low-grade fever, arterial partial pressure of oxygen below 65 mmHg, and chest radiographs demonstrating bilateral, interstitial shadowing.
A reduction in the circulating levels of all the major classes of immunoglobulin. is characterized by profound decreases in all classes of immunoglobulin with an absence of circulating B lymphocytes.

A type of renal tubular acidosis characterized by a failure of acid secretion by the alpha intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct of the distal nephron. The urine cannot be acidified below a pH of 5.3, associated with acidemia and hypokalemia.
An abnormally decreased potassium concentration in the blood.
A reduction in the proportion of CD4-positive T cells relative to the total number of T cells.
The presence of autoantibodies in the serum that react against proteins predominantly expressed in perinuclear region of neutrophils.

Atrophic gastritis (AG) is a histopathological entity that is characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa with loss of gastric glandular cells and replacement by intestinal-type epithelium, pyloric-type glands, and fibrous tissue.
Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck.
An extreme form of generalized edema with widespread and massive edema due to effusion of fluid into the extracellular space.
A type of lymphoma characterized microscopically by multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells.
Inflammation of the intestine leading to bacterial invasion causing cellular damage and death which causes necrosis of the colon and intestine.
An abnormal reduction of the relative proportion of CD4+ to CD8+ T cells.
Thickening of the heart walls in both ventricles.
Persistent presence of Epstein-Barr virus in the blood.
The presence of circulating IgG autoantibodies to cardiolipin.
An increased amount of calprotectin in the feces.
Periodic (episodic or recurrent) bouts of fever.
The enteric villi are atrophic or absent.
Increased susceptibility to viral infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of viral infection.
Any abnormality in the multiplication or reproduction of lymphocytes, which results in the expansion of a cell population.
Increased susceptibility to fungal infections, as manifested by multiple episodes of fungal infection.
Watery voluminous diarrhea resulting from an imbalance between ion and water secretion and absorption.
The presence of a rash (change of color and texture) of the perianal skin.
An unusually severe infection by cytomegalovirus.
An autoimmune form of hemolytic anemia.
Formation of calcium deposits in any soft tissue.
An increased concentration of pyruvate in the blood.
An abnormally high value of the serum anion gap (the sum of serum chloride and bicarbonate concentrations subtracted from the serum sodium concentration).
A reduced concentration of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate(2-) in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). 5-methyltetrahydrofolate is the active folate metabolite.

The presence of one or more obsessive-compulsive personality traits. Obsessions refer to persistent intrusive thoughts, and compulsions to intrusive behaviors, which the affected person experiences as involuntary, senseless, or repugnant.
Evidence of chronic denervation on electromyography.
Inner aspect of the upper lip vermilion (normally apposing the teeth) visible in a frontal view, i.e., the presence of an everted upper lip.
Any structural abnormality of the cerebral cortex.
Intrauterine growth retardation that is at least 2 standard deviations (SD) below average, but not as low as 3 SD, corrected for sex and gestational age.
A state characterized by a feeling of weakness and loss of strength leading to a generalized weakness of the body.

A mode of inheritance that is observed for dominant traits related to a gene encoded on the X chromosome. In the context of medical genetics, X-linked dominant disorders tend to manifest very severely in affected males. The severity of manifestation in females may depend on the degree of skewed X inactivation.
Syndactyly with fusion of toes four and five.
Absence of the middle phalanx of the middle (3rd) finger.
Absence of the distal phalanx of the middle (3rd) finger.
Absence of the middle phalanx of the index (2nd) finger.
Toes that appear disproportionately long compared to the foot.
Small, underdeveloped vertebral bodies.
Syndactyly with fusion of fingers two to five.
The presence of abnormal punctate (speckled, dot-like) calcifications in one or more epiphyses.
Aplasia of a toe. That is, absence of all phalanges of a non-hallux digit of the foot and the associated soft tissues.
Any deviation from the normal concentration of cholesterol in the blood circulation.
Reduced length of the clavicles.
Formation of an anuclear keratin layer
Absence or underdevelopment of tissue in the central nervous system.
The presence of only one working lower chamber in the heart, usually with a virtual absence of the ventricular septum and usually present in conjunction with double inlet left or right ventricle.
A morphological abnormality of a digit, i.e., of a finger or toe.
Unusual gonadal development in a person with a 46,XY male karyotype, leading to a more female sex differentiation.
Developmental hypoplasia of the fallopian tube.
Unusual gonadal development in a person with a 46,XY male karyotype, leading to an unassigned sex differentiation.
The presence of a gonadoblastoma, a neoplasm of a gonad that consists of aggregates of germ cells and sex cord elements.
An abnormality of the epididymis.
The presence of a dysgerminoma, i.e., an undifferentiated germ cell tumor of the ovary.
An abnormality of the conduction of electrical impulses by peripheral (motor or sensory) nerves. This finding is elicited by a nerve conduction study (NCS).
An abnormality of the myelination of motor and sensory peripheral nerves. These are axons for motor nerves and dendrites for sensory nerves in the strict anatomic sense.
Development of the reproductive system is inconsistent with the chromosomal sex.
An cystic ovarian teratoma composed of dermal and epidermal elements and containing tissue components including hair, teeth, bone, thyroid, and others.
An area of fat accumulation at the back of the neck in the form of a hump.
The presence of one or more cysts of the ovary.
A rounded, puffy face with fat deposits in the temporal fossa and cheeks, a double chin.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the esophagus.
A benign biphasic tumor of the breast with epithelial and stromal components.
A neoplasm originating in the pharynx.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of a gonad.
The presence of a neoplasm of the testis.

Nodular changes affecting the eyelids may have many different causes such as cystic lesions (chalaziae, hordeolae), lipogranulomas, melanomas, infectious diseases (Molluscum contagiosum) and many more.
Abnormally increased body weight.
Excessive fat around the stomach and abdomen.
A benign nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells.

Overproduction of the hormone of cortisol by the adrenal cortex, resulting in a characteristic combination of clinical symptoms termed Cushing syndrome, with truncal obesity, a round, full face, striae atrophicae and acne, muscle weakness, and other features.

The presence of abnormally increased levels of prolactin in the blood. Prolactin is a peptide hormone produced by the anterior pituitary gland that plays a role in breast development and lactation during pregnancy.

Acromegaly is a condition resulting from overproduction of growth hormone by the pituitary gland in persons with closed epiphyses, and consists chiefly in the enlargement of the distal parts of the body. The circumference of the skull increases, the nose becomes broad, the tongue becomes enlarged, the facial features become coarsened, the mandible grows excessively, and the teeth become separated. The fingers and toes grow chiefly in thickness.
A cystic tumor of the ovary, containing thin, clear, yellow serous fluid and varying amounts of solid tissue.

A myxoma (tumor of primitive connective tissue) of the heart. Cardiac myxomas consist of stellate to plump, cytologically bland mesenchymal cells set in a myxoid stroma. Cardiac myxomas are of endocardial origin and general project from the endocardium into a cardiac chamber.
Presence of abnormal cells inside a milk duct, that is, non-invasive breast cancer. Ductal carcinoma in situ is considered to be a precursor lesion to invasive breast cancer.
A tumor that originates in the paranasal sinus.
Hypercortisolemia associated with a primary defect of the adrenal gland leading to overproduction of cortisol.
A solitary, benign, intramedullary cartilage tumor that is often found in the short tubular bones of the hands and feet, distal femur, and proximal humerus.
The concentration of corticotropin, also known as adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), is below the lower limit of normal in the blood circulation.
An elevated level of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) in the blood circulation.
The presence of an follicular adenocarcinoma of the thyroid gland.
A myxoma originating in the skin.

Inability to be weaned from intravenous (parenteral) nutrition, as judged by the hydration status (urine output, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, urine sodium concentration), ability to maintain weight, stool output, and serum electrolyte status.
Acute obstruction of the intestines preventing passage of the contents of the intestines.

A reduced concentration of prealbumin in the blood. Prealbumin, also known as transthyretin, has a half-life in plasma of about 2 days, much shorter than that of albumin. Prealbumin is therefore more sensitive to changes in protein-energy status than albumin, and its concentration closely reflects recent dietary intake rather than overall nutritional status.
Inflammation of the renal glomeruli.
The presence of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins) in the serum that react against thyroid peroxidase.
The presence of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins) in the serum that react against glutamic acid decarboxylase.
The presence of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins) in the serum that react against the insulin receptor.

Increased susceptibility to gastroenteritis, an infectious inflammationof the stomach and small intestines manifested by signs and symptoms such as diarheas and abdominal pain, as manifested by recurrent episodes of gastroenteritis.

Primary food allergies primarily occur as a result (most likely) of gastrointestinal sensitization to predominantly stable food allergens (glycoproteins). A secondary food allergy develops after primary sensitization to airborne allergens (e. g., pollen allergens) with subsequent reactions (due to cross-reactivity) to structurally related often labile allergens in (plant) foods.
The presence of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins) in the serum that react against a 60-kd peptide contained in the liver cytosolic fraction.
A type of hemolytic anemia in which the Coombs test is positive.
Inflammation of the thyroid gland.
A type of infection that is regarded as a sign of a pathological susceptibility to infection because of unusual severity or intensity of the infection.
Abnormality of the homeostasis (concentration) of a monoatomic ion.
An abnormally decreased proportion of CD4-negative, CD8-negative (double negative or DN) alpha-beta regulatory T cells (Tregs) as compared to total number of T cells.
The presence of inflammation of the gastric mucous membrane.
An abnormally decreased magnesium concentration in the blood.
Altered immune function characterized by lymphoid proliferation, immune activation, and excessive autoreactivity often leading to autoimmune/inflammatory complications.
The presence of inflammation of the skin. That is, an abnormality of the skin resulting from the local accumulation of fluid, plasma proteins, and leukocytes.
A type of glomerulonephropathy characterized by thickening of the basement membrane and deposition of immune complexes in the subepithelial space.
Paralysis of the facial nerves on the basis of overgrowth of the cranial bones causing impingement upon the seventh cranial nerve.
Syndactyly with fusion of fingers two and three.
An abnormality of the development of the fingernails.
Lack of sharpness of vision resulting in the inability to see fine detail.
Sclerosis (abnormal hardening) of cortical bone, characterized by increased radiodensity.
An elevation in bone density in one or more diaphyses. Sclerosis is normally detected on a radiograph as an area of increased opacity.
Excessive growth of the bones of cranium, i.e., of the skull.
Increased width (cross-sectional diameter) of the clavicles.
Increased thickness (diameter) of ribs.
An abnormal increased concentration of parathyroid hormone.
Excessive growth of the craniofacial bones.
An abnormal increase of bone mineral density with generalized involvement of the skeleton.
Sclerosis (increased density) affecting vertebral end plates.
Increased density of the compact bone of long bone.
An abnormal narrowing of the external auditory canal.
Onset of disease at an age of greater than or equal to 19 to under 25 years.
Abnormally increased density of craniofacial bone tissue.

Deviated fingers is a term that should be used if one or more fingers of the hand are deviated from their normal position, either to the radial or ulnar side. A deviation of a finger can be caused by an abnormal form of one or more of the phalanges of the affected finger, or by a deviation or displacement of one or more phalanges.
A spinal cord hemangioma located in the lumbosacral spine region.
Benign neoplasia derived from lipoblasts or lipocytes of white or brown fat. May be angiomatous or hibernomatous.
The presence of a leiomyoma of the uterus.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the adenohypophysis, which is also known as the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland.
A bilateral vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neurinoma).
The presence of a peripheral schwannoma.
A neoplasm affecting the spinal cord.
The presence of a meningioma, i.e., a benign tumor originating from the dura mater or arachnoid mater.
Reduced intensity (volume) of speech.
Muscular weakness and atrophy related to loss of the motor neurons of the spinal cord and brainstem.

An abnormal change (metaplasia) in the cells of the inferior portion of the esophagus. The normal squamous epithelium lining of the esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium. Columnar epithelium refers to a cell type that is typically found in more distal parts of the gastrointestinal system.
A reduction in the number of axons in the peripheral nervous system.
Defect in the epithelium of the esophagus, essentially an open sore in the lining of the esophagus.
The presence of a carcinoma of the esophagus.
Wasting of the tongue.
Irregularities of the iliac crest that produce the appearance of a lace border around it.

A developmental defect of the sacrum characterized by partial or disordered development of the sacrum in which portions of the sacrum, which normally is formed by fusion of five sacral vertebrae S1-S5, fail to form or fail to form normally.
Metaphyseal cupping refers to an inward bulging of the metaphyseal profile giving the metaphysis a cup-like appearance.
A shift from the normally round (convex) appearance of the iliac wing towards a square-like appearance.
Absence of the mandible.
Weakness of the cartilage in the trachea and the bronchi, resulting in a floppy (non-rigid) airway. Affected persons may have difficulties to maintain patency of the airways.

An abnormal inversion (turning inward) of the eyelid (usually the lower) towards the globe. Entropion is usually acquired as a result of involutional or cicatricial processes but may occasionally be congenital.
Absence of the clavicles as a developmental defect.
Supernumerary digits located at the ulnar side of the hand with a complete extra finger and extra metacarpal.
Increased sensitivity to stimulation, excluding the special senses, which may refer to various modes of cutaneous sensibility including touch and thermal sensation without pain, as well as to pain.
Gradual, very slow onset of disease manifestations.
Double rows of eyelashes.
A type of hearing impairment caused by an abnormal functionality of the cochlear nerve with congenital onset.
An increased amount of nitrogen in the form of urea in the blood.
A congenital malformation with a cleft (gap or opening) in the face.
Reduction in diameter of the internal auditory canal.
Abnormality of the adrenal glands, i.e., of the endocrine glands located at the top of the kindneys.
An abnormality of the middle ear.
Bony fusion of malleus, incus, and stapes.
Facial height (length) is more than two standard deviations below the mean (objective); or an apparent decrease in the height (length) of the face (subjective).
A subjective feeling that an experience which is occurring for the first time has been experienced before.
A focal cognitive seizure with forced thinking characterized by retained awareness throughout the seizure.
A type of focal sensory seizure with auditory features during which awareness is retained throughout the seizure.
A focal autonomic seizure with epigastric sensation / nausea / vomiting / other gastrointestinal phenomena characterized by retained awareness throughout the seizure.
An early onset of puberty, in this case early does not refer to precocious.
Abnormal narrowing of the coronary artery.
A detrimental reaction to a food, beverage, food additive, or compound found in foods that produces symptoms in one or more body organs and systems that is not mediated by an immune reaction.
Delay or absence of the swallow response, reflexes triggered by the contact the food bolus makes with the anterior faucial pillars.
Increased muscle tone observed in the arms of the affected person.
Underdevelopment of the ventral portion of the pons.
An increase in size of the anatomic space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater in the region surrounding the cerebellum.
A type of spasticity that affects one or more limbs (arms or legs).
Recurrent episodes of sustained upward deviation of the eyes and incomplete downward saccades, and normal horizontal eye movements without impairment of consciousness.

A short generalized seizure, of a duration of <15 min, not recurring within 24 h, occurring during a febrile episode not caused by an acute disease of the nervous system intracranial infection or severe metabolic disturbance.
Episodic fever that recurs at regular intervals.
A reduction from normal of the mean corpuscular volume, or mean cell volume (MCV) of red blood cells (usually defined as an MCV below 80 femtoliters).
The presence of an abnormal number of fragmented red blood cells (schistocytes) in the blood.

An epiretinal membrane is a thin sheet of fibrous tissue that can develop on the surface of the macular area of the retina and cause a disturbance in vision. An epiretinal membrane area can develop on the thin macular area of the retin. An epiretinal membrane is also sometimes called a macular pucker, premacular fibrosis, surface wrinkling retinopathy or cellophane maculopathy.
The presence of elliptical, cigar-shaped erythrocytes on peripheral blood smear.

A phalangeal malformation that is termed angel-shaped phalanx (ASP), because of its resemblance to the angels used for decoration of Christmas trees. The various components of an angel-shaped phalanx are: diaphyseal cuff (wings), surrounding a meta-diaphyseal core (body), which may appear empty or structured with a cone-shaped epiphysis (skirt) and pseudoepiphysis (head).
An abnormality of the structure or form of the diaphysis, i.e., of the main or mid-section (shaft) of a long bone.
A type of cirrhosis characterized by the presence of small regenerative nodules.
Lack of strength of the proximal muscles that becomes progressively more severe.
Any structural abnormality or abnormal count of granulocytes.

An abnormal increase in intracellular lipid droplets In a muscle. The number and size of these drops can increase with somd disorders of lipid metabolism affecting muscle. See PMID 20691590 for histological images.
An abnormality of the mitochondria in muscle tissue.
A lighter than expected T2 signal on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brainstem. This term refers to a localized hyperintensity affecting a particular region of the brainstem.
A disorder of the cardiac conduction system of the heart characterized by ventricular preexcitation due to the presence of an abnormal accessory atrioventricular electrical conduction pathway.
Moving another person's hand, body part, or body to communicate a desire, e.g. pushing or pulling someone toward a desired object or placing someone's hand on something.
Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e.g., strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interests).
Difficulty initiating sleep, that is, increased sleep onset latency, refers to the condition where it takes 30 minutes or more to fall asleep.

Any type of seizure (most often a generalized tonic-clonic seizure) occurring with fever (at least 38.0 degrees Celsius) but in the absence of central nervous system infection, severe metabolic disturbance or other alternative precipitant in people beyond the typical arrange of 3 months-6 years with no prior history of afebrile seizure.

Increased dimensions of the Virchow-Robin spaces (also known as perivascular spaces), which surround the walls of vessels as they course from the subarachnoid space through the brain parenchyma. Perivascular spaces are commonly microscopic, and not visible on conventional neuroimaging. This term refers to an increase of size of these spaces such that they are visible on neuroimaging (usually magnetic resonance imaging). The dilatations are regular cavities that always contain a patent artery.
A transient reduction in the number of neutrophils in the peripheral blood. Transient neutropenia is most commonly associated with viral infections, but other causes include drugs and autoimmunity.
Neutropenia with an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) less than 1,500,000,000/L lasting for more than 3 months.
A reduced concentration of Vitamin D.
Irregularity of the normally smooth surface of the proximal metaphysis of the femur.

Hemoglobin F (HbF) contains two globin alpha chains and two globin gamma chains. It is the main form of hemoglobin in the fetus during the last seven months of intrauterine development and in the half year of postnatal life. In adults it normally makes up less than one percent of all hemoglobin. This term refers to an increase in HbF above this limit. In beta thalassemia major, it may represent over 90 percent of all hemoglobin, and in beta thalassemia minor it may make up between 0.5 to 4 percent.
Abnormally increased density of metaphyseal bone.
Concentration of vitamin A below the lower limit of normal in the blood circulation.
A deficiency in the intake of energy and nutrients.
Abnormal widening of the metaphyseal regions of long bones.

Abnormally increased size of the costochondral junctions, which are located between the distal part of the ribs and the costal cartilages, which are bars of hyaline cartilage that connect the ribs to the sternum.
Malformation of the rib cage.
An abnormality of skeletal development characterized by a disturbance of the metaphysis and its histological structure with relatively normal epiphyses and vertebrae.
An impairment of the migration of neutrophils towards chemoattractants as part of the innate immune response

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is defined as a posterior and inferior slippage of the proximal epiphysis of the femur onto the metaphysis (femoral neck), occurring through the physeal plate during the early adolescent growth spurt.
A purpuric lesion that is larger than 1 cm in diameter.
Irreversible damage to heart tissue (myocardium) due to lack of oxygen after a heart attack (myocardial infarction).
Hemorrhage occurring within the retina.
A reduced number of reticulocytes in the peripheral blood.
The presence of moderately increased concentrations of albumin in the urine, defined as and albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR) of 30 to 299 mg/gm (3.4 to 34 mg/mmol).
An anomaly in the metabolism of a vitamin.
An decreased concentration of cholesterol in the blood.
An abnormal increase in the amount of intracellular lipid droplets in hepatocytes.
The natural longitudinal (posterodistal) convex arch is not present or is inverted.
Prominent glomerular basement membrane (GBM), reflecting an increase in thickness (subjective estimate) of the basal lamina of the glomerulus of the kidney.
A deviation from the normal count of B cells, i.e., the cells that are formed in the bone marrow, migrate to the peripheral lymphatic system, and mature into plasma cells or memory cells.
Increased susceptibility to staphylococcal infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of staphylococcal infections.
A circumscribed area of pus or necrotic debris in the liver.
Increased susceptibility to streptococcal infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of streptococcal infections.
Any deviation from the normal overall count of natural killer (NK) cells in the circulation or a deviation from the normal distribution of NK cell subtypes.
Increased susceptibility to streptococcus pneumoniae infections as manifested by a history of recurrent infections by streptococcus pneumoniae.
Restless Leg Syndrome (RLS) is a condition characterized by an uncomfortable and restless sensation in the legs that occurs after going to bed, often leading to insomnia.
Underdevelopment of the macula lutea.
An abnormal reduction in the amount of pigmentation (reduced or absent) of skin, hair and eye (iris and retina).
Laminar thickening of skin.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the skin.
Abnormal decussation of the visual pathways, typically identified using visual evoked potentials (VEP) (asymmetrical distribution of the VEP over the posterior scalp).
Underdevelopment of the fovea centralis.
An infection of the lung caused by environmental mycobacteria. Such infections can occur in individuals with predisposing lung disease or immune disease.
An increased susceptibility to Aspergillus infections, as manifested by a history of recurrent episodes of Aspergillus infections.
Obstruction of the intestine due to abnormally thick meconium.
Aplasia (congenital absence) of the vas deferens.

Abnormally decreased weight-to-height squared ratio, calculated by dividing the individual's weight in kilograms by the square of the individual's height in meters and used as an indicator of underweight compared to averages.
An increased concentration of chloride in the sweat.
Increased susceptibility to infections with Burkholderia cepacia, as manifested by recurrent episodes of infection with this agent.
Increased susceptibility to Haemophilus influenzae infections as manifested by recurrent episodes of infection by Haemophilus influenzae.
Complete loss of hearing related to a sensorineural defect.
Any deviation from the normal concentration of a carbohydrate in the urine.
An abnormality of the composition of urine or the levels of its components.
A deviation from the normal concentration of a carbohydrate in the blood circulation.
An abnormality affecting the carpal bones of the wrist (scaphoid, lunate, triquetral, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate).
Intrauterine growth retardation that is 4 or more standard deviations below average, corrected for sex and gestational age.
Hypoplastic/small middle phalanx of the fifth finger.
